chapter_theme: Songs at Chidambaram (புலியூர்): the poet confesses his fall to courtesans who sell themselves, the pomp of wealth that vanishes in a moment, the life that runs from the womb to Death, and the confusion of the Vedas and sects; he asks for the reality beyond form and the formless, for the lamp of knowledge rather than an ascetic's outward marks, and for the yogic ascent to the dancing Lord's hall.
structure_note: Most songs follow the two halves and end at Puliyur. The confessions are of women (495, 498, 500, 501, 503, 504, 507), of pomp (499), of the life cycle (508) and of birth (505). 496 and 506 are yogic pleas, 497 sets inner knowledge against outward austerity, and 502 is a call for Murugan to come. The praise draws on the Chidambaram dance: the serpent sage and the tiger-footed sage who watch it (501, 502).

494.reading: The poet asks to be spared the trouble of being carried off by merciless Death with his twisted rope swung at the head, and the turmoil of reciting Vedas and many shastras while the six sects quarrel one after another; he asks for the reality that has form, beyond the formless and the formed. The praise names Murugan nephew of Hari, the treasure of Parvati, Kumaresa of Puliyur where the god who wears river, moon, konrai and serpent dances, who fought the Nirudar to powder in the sea, and who never even in dreams knows anger toward those who bow at his feet.
494.nuance: அறுவகை சமயம் முறைமுறை சருவி, the six sects quarrelling in turn, sits beside Death's rope as a second torment: the plea is for one true object (வடிவுள பொருள்) beyond அருவுரு. The line அலைபடு தநல்முச் சினையாகும் does not split cleanly and may be corrupt.

495.reading: The poet describes a courtesan from lips, smile, eyes, hair and brows down to breasts, navel, waist, thighs and feet, then frankly the lovemaking on the couch with sweating faces and bird-like cries, and asks Murugan to give him another thought and rule him, since he has lost all self-control. The praise is a long battle with drums and rivers of blood, the vel thrown at the northern mountain, the gods and Vidyadharas singing and apsaras dancing, Puliyur as a golden land of groves, tanks and birds, and Murugan's union with Valli and Devayanai.
495.nuance: The plea is one phrase at the end of the confession: வசமெலாம் விட்டு மறவே, having let go of all control, வேறு சிந்தனையைத் தந்து ஆள்வாய், give me a different thought. The head-to-foot catalogue is the stock form of these songs, here carried to its greatest length. One word is corrupt (see source_issues).

496.reading: A yogic plea: the poet asks to reach the golden place that neither darkness nor the sun's ray can touch, where his two ills burn, impurity leaves, the light at the root shines and nectar flows like a stream, so that Murugan's grace becomes his whole measure and Siva rejoices; and he asks for the feet. The praise names Siva as the supreme teacher who has no teacher, with moon and coral body, and Murugan as his son, who said of the poet 'this dog is my servant' and gave him true knowledge, at Puliyur, lover of the hunter girl.
496.nuance: The ascent is told in the language of Tirumular's yoga: மூலக ஒளி, the light at the base, and அமுதம் welling as an அருவி. இருநோய், the two diseases, is most likely the two kinds of deed (இருவினை); that is a guess. மருவி நாயெனை அடிமையாம் என is the book's formula of being taken into service.

497.reading: The poet asks not to wander the whole earth wearing ochre, growing matted hair, entering forests, living on raw fruit and punishing the body, but to be given Murugan's cool lotus feet so that he may see the lamp of supreme knowledge that dawns when the self and the elements subside. The praise names the fierce hero who ruined the sinful Daruka clan, the vel whose ghouls clap and sing, and the peacock dancing, at Puliyur among groves and bending paddy.
497.nuance: சீவ னொடுக்கம் பூத வொடுக்கம், the stilling of the self and of the elements, is what the outward marks of the ascetic fail to bring. The song does not condemn ascetics; it says this is not the path the poet asks for.

498.reading: The poet describes courtesans who comb flowers into their hair, sing like cuckoos, act coy, gather asking 'will money come?', run through the streets in deceit, and join with many at once to some men's ruin, and asks whether such company is fitting. The praise names the vel that struck the Suras, Murugan who knocked the Veda-maker on the head with his kanthal hand, the son of Uma who sits beside the one who burned Kama and wears the tiger skin, and Valli as the deer whose grace kindles the yogic fire at the root and the nada, at Puliyur, the land of Siva-knowledge.
498.nuance: பொருள் வருமோ, 'will money come?', and விலைமாதர் mark these as courtesans. The praise gives Valli a yogic role unusual in the book: she grants grace so that the light at the root (சுடர் மூலத்தோன்) is kindled and the life joins the breath in the nadi; the syntax is not certain. One word is corrupt.

499.reading: The poet describes the pomp of wealth: a palanquin under champak umbrellas, servants, silk, drums, veena and conch, armies and music, and says that this false show vanishes in a moment; instead of wandering in it he asks for the feet that are hard even for the gods to reach. The praise turns the Asura host to dust with the vel amid drum syllables and roaring seas, names Murugan son of Uma, whom Hara, Hari and Brahma cannot reach, and his union with the deer's daughter, at Puliyur.
499.nuance: இது நொடி மறையும் பொய்ப் பவுஷு, this false pomp that vanishes in a moment, is the whole argument. The song is unusual in confessing not women but status. The words விருமஞ்சித் திரமமா do not split clearly.

500.reading: The poet, calling himself the lowest dog, describes a woman's neck, eyes, brows, perfumes, breasts, waist and anklets and his union with her, and asks instead to win praise by bowing at Murugan's anklets, wearing holy ash and bathing in the waters of bliss like ascetics, worshipping his feet today. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, Murugan as guru to the consort of Gauri who dances, the gods showering flowers crying 'Kanda', and his union with the gypsy girl, at Puliyur where the golden dance is held.
500.nuance: The plea sets one bodily practice against another: ஒண்பொடி அணிந்து, wearing the bright ash, and ஆநந்தம் புனல் படிந்து, bathing in bliss, against the perfumed body of the confession. கவுரிபங்கன் குருவெனும் makes Murugan Siva's teacher. The rhythm packs the words tightly and several splits are uncertain.

501.reading: The poet tells how he smelled women's perfumed hair, lay on their breasts and lived proudly in pleasure, drawn to them like a needle to a magnet, and asks whether a day will come when grace fills him and, knowing without reasoning, he wears Murugan's faultless lotus feet. The praise names Siva, whom Vishnu and Brahma could not know, dancing before the serpent sage and the tiger-footed sage, wearing the half moon in his matted hair in the golden city, and Murugan as his treasure, at Puliyur with its golden walls.
501.nuance: காந்தமொடு ஊசி, needle and lodestone, is the image of compulsion. பாம்புருவான முநி and புலியான பதன் are Patanjali and Vyaghrapada, the two sages for whom Siva danced at Chidambaram; the song names them by their marks, not their names.

502.reading: The poet calls Murugan to come with his six faces shining from the mountain of ancient knowledge, his lips speaking the Veda, his anklets ringing, mounted on the peacock with the vel, so that the poet's two deeds turn to ash and the gods sing of the wonder. The praise names Siva who swallowed the poison when the gods fled, Murugan as the guru who gave him direct experience (அநுபூதி), the embracer of the hunter girl who drives off troubles and disease, praised by the tiger-footed sage, the serpent sage and countless rishis.
502.nuance: அடியன் இருவினை நீறுபட, that the servant's two deeds become ash, is the only plea; the rest is a vision of Murugan's coming. குருநாதன் மிகமகிழ அநுபூதி அருள்வோனே again makes Murugan the teacher of Siva.

503.reading: The poet describes courtesans who talk like parrots, invite a man with 'the house is free now, come', lead him to the bed, perfume him, and make love to him frankly described; when both have drowned in infatuation they pawn his ornaments and plunder his wealth, and he asks whether such lovemaking is right. The praise is a long litany of the Goddess as Shakti, Kalyani, Abhirami, Sivakami and Uma who dances with the Supreme, and of Murugan who rode the peacock, threw the Shakti and freed the gods, Valli's husband, who dwells in the minds of those who chant his name, Subramanya at Puliyur.
503.nuance: ஆபரணம் வைத்து அடகு தேடு பொருள் சூறைகொளுவார்: the women pawn his jewels and loot his goods once infatuation has taken him, the courtesan's stock charge. The Goddess is called எனை ஈண மலைமாது, the mountain daughter who bore me. One word is corrupt.

504.reading: The poet describes saleswomen who dance like peacocks with swinging breasts and parrot voices, and asks whether he must wander, quarrelling and making love with such harlots, until he coughs, vomits and hiccups like a mangy dog while people say 'chi chi'. The praise sets the vel against the Asuras amid drum syllables, names Murugan son of Sivakami and of the Lord who kicked Death, and his union with the deer born of Achyuta, who burned the southern demons' island, at Puliyur.
504.nuance: The confession runs straight from the women to disease and disgust (சிச்சி சிச்சி என நால்வர் கூறிட), with no interval. The phrase about Achyuta is corrupt; the sense that Valli is Vishnu's daughter is a guess from tradition.

505.reading: The poet, a dog lamenting 'will birth never end?', asks that if it is his deeds that keep his mind from reaching the holy hall, Murugan come in grace as he stands crying with a dry mouth, end the anxiety of his mind, and appear before him as he comes worshipping. The praise names Uma who sits on the skin seat, Murugan as the nectar friend of those who praise him, wearer of kadamba, husband of Valli the form of knowledge, the treasure of Puliyur, who raised up the gods.
505.nuance: திருச்சபை is the hall of the dance at Chidambaram: the poet's goal is to reach it in mind. வாய்பாறி நிற்கும், standing with mouth dried from crying, is the posture of the plea.

506.reading: A yogic plea: the poet asks when, from the fire in the four-cornered root lotus, through the nadis and mantras, past the moon and the six junctions, with the conch-like sound of bindu and nada at the front, he will drink the gods' nectar and reach the hall of the countless dances. The praise names the Goddess who removed his delusion of anava, kali and desire and ruled him, Murugan as her son, the vel that burned the deceivers' homes and drank the eight seas, and Siva who dances at south Puliyur.
506.nuance: நாலுசதுரத்த ... மூலகமலம் is the four-sided base lotus (muladhara) of the yogic body, and விந்துநாதம் the bindu and nada of Tirumular's teaching; the goal is the dance hall (சபை), set inside the body. ஆணவ மயக்கம் names the root impurity. The ascent's stages are not clear to me, and one word is corrupt.

507.reading: The poet describes women with dark hair, pearl-adorned lips, moon foreheads and carp eyes and asks whether he must wander daily at their command; he asks for release, so that his mind may hold to Murugan's feet with true knowledge. The praise names Uma at length and Murugan as the one who told the meaning of the light to Siva with the trident and fiery body, and his union with the deer of the three Tamils, at Puliyur.
507.nuance: சோதிப்பொருள் கேள்விக்கிடு முருகோனே, Murugan who gave Siva the meaning of the light to hear, is the story of the teaching of Siva; Om is not named. கட்டளையாக, at their command, makes the women masters and the poet a servant.

508.reading: The poet traces life from a drop like dew, ten months upside down in the womb, birth, crawling and toddling, to falling into the pit of women and leaving the body unawares when cunning Death comes, and asks whether this weakening sorrow of illusion will never end. The praise names the vel that powdered the mountain of illusion and dried the sea, Murugan as the guru who knocked Brahma's four heads, and husband of the lady who enters the minds of those who think of him, the fullness of Puliyur.
508.nuance: The whole life is told in eight short lines, and the only adult act is falling into women (மாதர்க் குழி விழுவார்) before Death arrives. மாயத்துயர், the sorrow of illusion, names the whole cycle.

links.note: The Kural says neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 497 asks to be spared ochre, matted hair, forest wandering and fasting and to be given instead the inner knowledge in which the self subsides. Both set the ascetic's outward marks aside, the Kural for conduct, 497 for grace and knowledge.
Both run a life from the womb through infancy and youth to women and then decline without pause; 9 ends in disease, 508 in Death's arrival, and both ask for release from the cycle.

The song asks to be spared the turmoil of the six sects quarrelling in turn (அறுவகை சமய முறைமுறை சருவி) and of reciting shastras, and to be given the one real object (வடிவுள பொருள்). Tirumanthiram 1558 says the six sects are six roads to one city (ஒன்றது பேரூர் வழியாறு), and those who say 'this is good, that is bad' are dogs barking at a hill. The verse supplies the reason the song's quarrel is futile: the roads lead to the same place.

The song lays out a woman from head to foot, her smile nectar and gems (அமுர்த மாணிக்க நகை), and only at the end asks to be given another thought (வேறு சிந்தனையைத் தந்து ஆள்வாய்). Naladiyar 45 refuses exactly such talk of smiles as jasmine buds and pearls (முல்லை முகை முறுவல் முத்து), because the speaker has seen the teeth and bones scattered in the burning ground. The pairing shows what the song's 'different thought' looks like in practice.

The song asks for the place where nectar wells like a falling stream (அருவி பாய இனமுதம் ஊற) as impurity leaves and the light at the root shines. Tirumanthiram 2535 puts the same welling stream (ஊறும் அருவி) on a high summit, a tank that fills without a river. Both use the spring on the height for the nectar of yogic ascent.

The song links the flow of nectar to the leaving of impurity (மலம் ஒழியவே ... அமுதம் ஊற). Tirumanthiram 800 says that when the sky-river is let into the tank, the one who looks up is free of dirt (அழுக்கற்ற வாறே). Both make the inner flood the cleansing itself.

The song asks not to wander wearing ochre and matted hair, but to see the lamp of knowledge that comes when self and elements subside (சீவனொடுக்கம் பூதவொடுக்கம்). Tirumanthiram 1660 grants that any garb, false or true, saves only those who have understood (உய்வேடமாகும் உணர்ந்தறிந்தோர்க்கே). The verse names the condition under which the song's rejected marks would still have worth.

The song's women gather asking 'will money come?' (பொருள் வருமோ) and join with many at once. Naladiyar 374 says that to such women a man without money is poison, while even an oil-presser who has earned wealth (செய்த பொருளுடையார்) is sugar. Both make money the only question these women ask of a man.

The song pictures the pomp of wealth, a palanquin under umbrellas (குடை சூழ் சிவிகை) with armies (பலபடை) and music, and calls it a false show that vanishes in a moment (நொடி மறையும் பொய்ப் பவுஷு). Naladiyar 3 shows men who rode under the umbrella at the head of armies (குடைநிழற்கீழ்ச் சேனைத் தலைவராய்) fallen when their deeds run out. Same emblems, same verdict.

The song's pomp is a palanquin (சிவிகை) with attendants, which it says vanishes in a moment. Tirumanthiram 149 shows a man who gained a palanquin and rode it in the square (சிவிகைபெற்றேறினான்), and did not turn back when the cry came that he had gone. Both use the palanquin as the sign of a status that does not last.

The song's wealth is a procession of drums, veena and conch that vanishes in a moment. Kural 332 compares great wealth to the crowd gathering at a dance hall (கூத்தாட்டு அவைக் குழாத்து) and its going to that crowd dispersing. The Kural gives the reason the song's noisy show is the right image for wealth: it is a gathered audience.

Against the perfumed body of the confession, the song asks to wear the bright ash (ஒண்பொடி அணிந்து) and bathe in bliss like ascetics (தவசர் சந்தம் போலும்). Tirumanthiram 1662 names wearing ash (பூதி அணிவது) as the first emblem of the Siva-yogi. The song takes the ascetic's first emblem as its sign of turning.

The song's praise names Siva dancing before the serpent-form sage and the tiger-footed one (பாம்புருவான முநி, வாம்புலியான பதன்) at Puliyur. Tirumanthiram 67 lists Patanjali and Vyaghra who worshipped at the hall (மன்று தொழுத பதஞ்சலி வியாக்ரமர்) among the masters who received Nandi's grace. The two sages of the Chidambaram dance are named by their marks in the song and by name in Tirumular.

Kural 5 says the two deeds born of darkness (இருள்சேர் இருவினை) do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise. The song asks Murugan to come so that his servant's two deeds turn to ash (அடியன் இருவினை நீறுபட) while the gods sing of the wonder. The song turns the Kural's 'do not cling' into a burning away at the god's coming.

The song's women, once both have drowned in infatuation (மயல் மூழ்கிய பின்), pawn his jewels and loot what he has (ஆபரணம் வைத்து அடகு தேடு பொருள் சூறைகொளுவார்). Naladiyar 377 says such a woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from a man's hand (கைப்பொருள் கொண்டு), then lies down like a balking ox. Both put the taking after the fondness.

The song's client ends coughing and hiccuping like a howling dog (ஊளை நாயென) while people say 'chi chi'. Naladiyar 375 calls the men who embrace women of double conduct dull-witted like beasts (விலங்கன்ன வெள்ளறிவினார்). Both turn the client, not the woman, into an animal.

The song cries 'will birth never end?' (பிறப்பு முடியாதோ) and asks for the unfading flower of the feet (வாடா மலர்ப்பதவி). Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்). The song is the Kural's claim spoken as a cry from inside the sea.

The song climbs from the root lotus (மூலகமலம்) through the nadis and mantras to drink the gods' nectar (வானவமுதத்தை உண்டு) and reach the hall of the dance. Tirumanthiram 2989 tells the seeker to pass through the lotus of the flesh (ஊனார் கமலத்தின் ஊடு) and beyond, and then drink honey to the full. Both are the same ascent from the body's lotus to a drink of sweetness.

At the top of the song's ascent bindu and nada sound like a conch (சங்கொலி விந்துநாதம்). Tirumanthiram 731 names bindu, the mantra and the abiding nada (மன்னிய நாதம்) as the yogi's path. The song uses Tirumular's terms for the same stages.

The song asks whether the poet must wander daily at the women's command (கட்டளையாக ... நித்தமும் உழல்வேனோ) instead of holding the feet with true knowledge. Kural 909 says virtue, wealth and other aims are absent in those who do a woman's bidding (பெண்ஏவல் செய்வார்). The Kural speaks of the husband and the wife; the song moves the same servitude to the courtesan and its loss to release.

The song runs from the womb to falling into the pit of women (மாதர்க் குழி விழுவார்) and to Death, and asks whether this sorrow of illusion (மாயத்துயர்) will never end. Tirumanthiram 185 says that after Death sets the base in the pit of the womb (கருக்குழி) they fall into it again, their bewilderment unending (திகைப்பொழியாரே). The two pits, of women and of the womb, are the same circle.

source_issues: Song 495: one corrupt character in இணைசொல்க்஡ண (line 9); probably க்ரீவ (neck), compared with the conch.
Song 498: one corrupt character in று஡ங்கமிலார் (line 8); probably றூங்கமிலார், but the word is unclear.
Song 503: one corrupt character in வாயிதழினு஡றல் (line 7); clearly ஊறல்.
Song 504: one corrupt character in அச்சுத஡ணன (line 23); the sense (perhaps அச்சுதன் ஈன்ற, 'born of Achyuta') is unclear.
Song 506: one corrupt character in இந்துவினு஡டுற (line 3); clearly இந்துவினூடுற.
Song 499: the words விருமஞ்சித் திரமமா (line 10) do not split into clear words and may be corrupt.
